CONFIDENCE: 95

Yes. Absolute productivity advantages do not rule out mutual gains. What matters is comparative advantage: each country should specialize in the good for which its opportunity cost is lower, then trade.

Suppose Country A produces both cars and wheat more efficiently than Country B, but the productivity gap is larger for cars than for wheat. Then A’s opportunity cost of wheat (cars forgone) is higher than B’s, so B has a comparative advantage in wheat and A in cars. If A specializes toward cars and B toward wheat, total world output of both goods can rise. Trade at a price between the two countries’ autarky opportunity costs lets each consume more of both goods than it could alone.

The same logic applies if the gap is larger for wheat instead: the labels reverse, but mutual gains remain possible. Gains fail only in the knife-edge case where opportunity-cost ratios are identical, so neither side has a comparative advantage.

CONFIDENCE: 96

Research finds that strict rent control mainly reduces the quantity and quality of rental housing, misallocates the existing stock, and helps incumbent tenants while harming newcomers and overall market efficiency.

Empirical studies (including work on San Francisco and other tightly controlled cities, plus broader reviews and economist surveys) show landlords respond by converting units to owner-occupied housing, withdrawing them from the rental market, or cutting maintenance. New supply is discouraged. Tenants who already hold controlled units gain lower rents and longer tenure, but mobility falls, units are not reallocated to households that value them most, shortages and queues grow, and uncontrolled segments often see higher rents. These effects are stronger under strict (near-freeze) controls than under milder stabilization rules.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. Removing lead from gasoline and restricting lead paint produced large, well-documented net gains in public health that far exceeded the compliance costs.

Lead is a potent neurotoxin with no safe exposure level, especially for young children. Before regulation, leaded gasoline and deteriorating lead paint were the dominant sources of population exposure in the United States and many other countries. After the U.S. phase-down of leaded gasoline (beginning in the 1970s and essentially complete by the mid-1990s) and the 1978 ban on lead paint in housing, average childhood blood-lead levels fell by more than an order of magnitude—from roughly 15 µg/dL in the late 1970s to well under 1 µg/dL in recent national surveys. Parallel declines occurred in other countries that adopted similar rules.

Those exposure reductions translated into measurable benefits: higher average cognitive scores, fewer cases of lead-related anemia and kidney and cardiovascular disease, and lower special-education and healthcare costs. Economic assessments (including EPA retrospective analyses and peer-reviewed estimates of avoided IQ loss) put the monetized benefits in the hundreds of billions of dollars, against industry transition costs measured in the low billions. The same pattern appears internationally wherever leaded fuel was eliminated.

Remaining lead hazards (old paint, contaminated soil, some industrial sources) still require attention, and the precise share of later crime declines attributable to lead is debated. Neither point reverses the central result: on health, cognitive, and economic grounds, the phase-out and paint rules were a clear net benefit.

CONFIDENCE: 92

Mostly U.S. importers, businesses, and consumers—not foreign exporters. The importer of record pays the tariff to U.S. Customs. Empirical work on recent U.S. tariffs (including Amiti, Redding, and Weinstein and related studies) finds near-complete pass-through into U.S. import prices, so the economic burden falls mainly on the American side rather than being absorbed through lower foreign prices.

CONFIDENCE: 85

No. Mass literacy in England was already largely in place before compulsory state schooling.

Signature literacy (the standard historical proxy, from parish marriage registers) stood at roughly two-thirds of men and half of women by the 1840s, and about 80% of men and 73% of women by 1871—before the 1870 Elementary Education Act created school boards and well before attendance was made compulsory (1880) and schooling free (1891). The long rise began in the early modern period and accelerated through private, charity, dame, and Sunday schools plus informal instruction in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. State grants to voluntary schools from 1833 and the later board-school system finished the remaining gaps and standardized provision; they did not produce the mass literate population.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Occupational licensing—government rules that require training, exams, fees, or other credentials before someone may legally work in a job—has been studied extensively by labor economists (notably Morris Kleiner and coauthors), federal agencies, and state policy researchers. For occupations such as barbers, cosmetologists, florists, and many contractor trades, the main documented effects are:

- **Higher earnings for licensed workers and higher prices for consumers.** Licensing restricts entry, producing a wage premium on the order of 10–15% on average and corresponding increases in service prices. Consumers pay more and, in some markets, face reduced availability.
- **Lower employment and slower entry.** Requirements deter people from entering the occupation, especially those with less money or time for schooling and fees. Employment in licensed fields is lower than it would otherwise be.
- **Reduced geographic mobility.** Because rules differ sharply across states, workers often cannot move and keep practicing without repeating costly requirements.
- **Weak or null effects on quality and safety in lower-risk fields.** For barbers, florists, interior designers, and similar occupations, studies generally find little or no measurable improvement in service quality, consumer complaints, or safety relative to unlicensed or less-regulated settings. (Evidence is more mixed for higher-risk trades such as some electrical or plumbing work, where safety externalities are clearer.)
- **Disparate burdens.** Costs fall more heavily on lower-income workers, immigrants, and people changing careers, while benefits accrue mainly to already-licensed incumbents.

These patterns appear consistently in the academic literature and in summaries such as the 2015 White House/Treasury/Labor report on occupational licensing. Licensing can still be justified where genuine public-safety risks are large and well-documented, but for the kinds of occupations cited in the question the dominant measured effects are higher prices, less entry, and little quality gain.

CONFIDENCE: 82

No. A 50-to-1 pay gap is not unfair simply because the numbers differ. People do not produce equal value, and pay in competitive labor markets largely tracks differences in skills, responsibility, scarcity, risk, and the revenue or savings someone’s work creates.

Measured productivity gaps are often large. In knowledge work, sales, surgery, software, and entertainment, top performers routinely generate many times the output of median workers; firm-size and “superstar” effects amplify that further for executives and public figures. A surgeon, founder, or specialist whose decisions move millions in value is not doing the same job as someone in a low-skill role with many substitutes. Equal pay for unequal contribution would itself be unfair to the higher contributor and to the customers or employers who voluntarily pay the premium.

That does not mean every large gap is justified. Some reflect monopoly power, cronyism, discrimination, or luck rather than contribution. Those cases are unfair because of how the money was obtained, not because the ratio crossed an arbitrary line such as 50. Fairness is about process and proportionality to value created, not about compressing outcomes to a preferred multiple.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Cities that introduced congestion pricing have generally found clear reductions in traffic volumes and congestion inside the charged zones (often on the order of 10–30%), faster and more reliable travel times, some shift toward public transit or off-peak trips, modest air-quality gains, and useful revenue—frequently reinvested in transport—while public acceptance tends to rise after the scheme is in place.

CONFIDENCE: 85

Research finds small or negligible effects overall. Comprehensive reviews (notably the 2017 National Academies of Sciences report) and most labor-economics studies conclude that immigration has little long-run impact on the wages of native-born workers as a group. Any negative effects that appear are concentrated on earlier immigrants (the closest substitutes) and, to a lesser extent, native-born high-school dropouts; even for that subgroup the estimated wage reductions are typically only a few percent and often statistically fragile once capital adjustment, occupational specialization, and longer time horizons are taken into account. A minority of studies (e.g., some work by Borjas) report larger short-run losses for the least-skilled natives, but these results are sensitive to methodology and are not the central tendency of the literature.

CONFIDENCE: 72

No. The shift away from lead in U.S. household paint was already well underway decades earlier and was driven by a mix of voluntary industry changes, cheaper non-lead pigments (especially titanium dioxide), and earlier rules—not by the 1978 CPSC ban.

Key points in the timeline:
- By the 1940s–1950s, manufacturers were already cutting lead content as health concerns grew and alternatives improved.
- In 1955 the industry adopted a voluntary standard capping lead at 1% in interior paints.
- The 1971 Lead-Based Paint Poisoning Prevention Act and a 1973 CPSC limit (0.5%) further reduced use before the final 1978 rule (0.06% for residential paint).

The 1978 action largely locked in and enforced a phase-out that had already occurred in new household paint; it did not initiate it. Homes built after about 1950, and especially after the early 1970s, therefore contain far less lead paint than older stock.

CONFIDENCE: 85

Yes. The clearest U.S. case is thalidomide in 1960–61. Under the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act’s pre-market safety requirement, FDA medical officer Frances Kelsey repeatedly refused to approve Richardson-Merrell’s application, demanding better evidence on safety (including in pregnancy). While she delayed approval, the drug was already causing thousands of severe birth defects in countries where it had been marketed. Once those harms became undeniable, the U.S. application was abandoned. Only limited investigational distribution occurred here, producing on the order of a dozen affected births rather than the mass epidemic seen in Europe (roughly 10,000 cases). That outcome is the standard historical demonstration that withholding marketing approval prevented widespread harm that the same compound caused where it was sold.

CONFIDENCE: 88

The legal incidence of the corporate income tax falls on corporations, but its economic incidence (who actually loses real income) does not. In standard public-finance models the burden is shared by owners of capital and by workers; consumers may also bear some of it through higher prices. The split depends on capital mobility, factor substitutability, and market structure.

In a closed economy the classic Harberger result assigns most of the long-run burden to capital owners economy-wide. In an open economy mobile capital can relocate, so a larger share is shifted onto labor via lower wages and onto landowners. Empirical estimates vary widely—commonly placing labor’s share anywhere from roughly one-quarter to well over half—but virtually all serious studies reject the claim that shareholders alone bear the tax.

CONFIDENCE: 72

No. Heritability is the fraction of observed variation in a trait, within a given population and range of environments, that is associated with genetic differences. It says nothing about how much the average level of the trait would shift if the environment changed, including by interventions outside the environments already sampled. Height, for example, is highly heritable yet has risen substantially across generations with better nutrition; the same logic applies to many other traits.

CONFIDENCE: 95

Yes. Vaccination often generates positive externalities that private decisions do not fully capture, so the privately chosen uptake rate can be below the social optimum.

An unvaccinated person raises infection risk for others, increases transmission chains, and can impose costs on healthcare systems, insurers, employers, and caregivers. Those costs are not fully priced into the individual’s choice, especially when the personal risk of severe disease is low. Herd immunity is closer to a public good: once coverage is high enough, further spread is suppressed for everyone, including people who cannot be vaccinated. Rational free-riding then predicts under-vaccination relative to the coverage that minimises total social cost.

Standard corrections follow. Subsidies (or free provision) lower the private price toward the social benefit and are the usual first tool when the main failure is an unpriced externality or liquidity/access constraint. Requirements—school-entry rules, occupational rules, or similar—are economically justified when voluntary uptake, even at a zero price, still falls short of the social optimum and the avoided epidemic or outbreak costs exceed the compliance and liberty costs. Both tools are context-specific: the case is strongest for contagious diseases with high external costs (measles, pertussis, many childhood vaccines; influenza and COVID in high-transmission settings) and weaker when a vaccine mainly protects the recipient and barely reduces transmission.

Empirical health-economics work generally supports this. Childhood immunisation programmes are repeatedly estimated to be cost-saving or highly cost-effective once averted medical care, productivity losses, and outbreak control are counted. Outbreaks after coverage collapses (for example measles) impose large, measurable public costs. Mandates have historically raised coverage where subsidies alone did not. The economic case is not identical to a medical case, and it does not imply every vaccine should be mandated; it does imply that “let people pay and choose” will often under-provide protection against contagious disease.

CONFIDENCE: 86

No. Within-group heritability only describes how much of the variation among individuals inside a given group is associated with genetic differences under that group’s environment. It says nothing, by itself, about the causes of a mean difference between groups.

A trait can be substantially heritable inside each of two groups while the entire gap between their averages is environmental. The standard illustrations are height (highly heritable within cohorts, yet secular gains are nutritional) and genetically similar seeds grown in rich versus poor soil (within-plot variation genetic, between-plot mean difference environmental). The same logic applies to IQ: shared or group-specific environments, measurement differences, or other non-genetic factors can shift averages without contradicting within-group heritability estimates.

Establishing a partial genetic contribution to a group mean difference requires separate evidence (for example, about the relevant genetic variants, their frequencies, and the environments), not an inference from within-group heritability alone.

CONFIDENCE: 92

Economic growth (rising adult wages and family incomes) plus technological change that cut demand for unskilled child workers. U.S. child employment (ages 10–15) had already fallen from roughly 18% in 1900 to about 5% by 1930—before the 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act—while compulsory-schooling rules and uneven state laws reinforced a decline already under way. Federal legislation largely locked in and completed that shift rather than causing it.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Personality traits such as extraversion and neuroticism are moderately heritable. Large twin, family, and adoption studies consistently estimate that genetic differences account for roughly 40–60% of the variance in these traits (often near the middle of that range), with the remainder attributable mainly to nonshared environment and measurement error rather than shared family environment. Molecular-genetic (SNP) estimates are lower, reflecting the usual “missing heritability” gap, but do not overturn the behavioral-genetic findings.

CONFIDENCE: 85

Yes. The Montreal Protocol worked: it drove a near-global phase-out of CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances, atmospheric concentrations of the main CFCs have fallen since the 1990s, and the Antarctic ozone hole is slowly healing, with full recovery toward 1980 levels expected around mid-century if compliance holds.

A treaty was required because ozone depletion is a global atmospheric commons problem. CFCs mix worldwide, last for decades, and destroy ozone far from where they are released, so one country’s emissions harm everyone. Unilateral bans would have been undercut by production shifting to non-participants and by competitive pressure on firms; only binding, near-universal rules, trade restrictions on non-parties, and assistance for developing countries could close that free-rider gap. Science (the Molina–Rowland mechanism, then the observed ozone hole) made the case urgent, and the protocol’s amendment process let controls tighten as evidence improved.

CONFIDENCE: 93

Yes. Smallpox eradication (certified in 1980) was achieved by the WHO’s Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme and cooperating national public-health systems: mass and ring vaccination, active case-finding, containment, and cross-border coordination, largely publicly financed and organized. Ordinary market activity alone was not a plausible route to the same outcome. Vaccination and especially eradication generate large positive externalities and free-rider problems; endemic transmission persisted in poor regions where private demand and supply would not have produced near-universal coverage or the surveillance-containment system required to drive incidence to zero and keep it there.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. Multinational export factories in poor countries generally pay *better* than the realistic local alternatives (subsistence farming, informal day labor, domestic firms), which is why workers queue for those jobs. Absolute wages look low by rich-country standards, but that is not the relevant comparison.

Cross-country and firm-level evidence (including foreign-owned vs. domestic plants, and apparel/footwear export zones vs. national averages) consistently finds wage premiums, often large, plus somewhat better enforcement of basic rules than in the informal sector. Workers’ revealed preference—staying, migrating toward the factories, and protesting closures—matches the wage data. Abuses and unsafe conditions occur and should be policed, but they do not overturn the pay comparison.

Boycotts and demand collapses do not help those workers. Lost orders mean layoffs or plant closures; the displaced typically move into lower-paid, more hazardous, or less stable work, not into better formal jobs that do not exist at scale. Historical cases (sudden loss of export orders after campaigns) show employment falling and child or informal labor rising, not conditions improving. Sustained gains come from productivity growth, more employers competing for labor, and broader development—not from shrinking the best available demand for that labor.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. Large, replicated average sex differences in vocational interests are among the most robust findings in psychology. A major meta-analysis (Su, Rounds & Armstrong, 2009) of interest inventories found that men score substantially higher on “things” orientations and women on “people” orientations (Cohen’s \(d \approx 0.93\) on the bipolar People–Things dimension). Parallel differences appear on the RIASEC scales that load on this dimension (e.g., Realistic \(d \approx 0.84\) favoring men; Social \(d \approx 0.68\) favoring women), with smaller or negligible gaps on other dimensions.  

These gaps emerge early, hold across decades of data and across dozens of countries (including highly gender-egalitarian ones), and predict real occupational choices (e.g., engineering vs. nursing/education). They are average differences with substantial within-sex overlap, not categorical rules, but their magnitude is large by conventional psychological standards and is not an artifact of a single instrument or culture.

CONFIDENCE: 90

Moderate city-level minimum-wage increases of 10–15% generally produce little or no detectable decline in overall employment. A large body of modern empirical work (event studies and difference-in-differences designs that track low-wage jobs across many state and local hikes) finds wage gains concentrated at the bottom of the distribution, with employment elasticities near zero; any job losses that appear are small, often statistically insignificant, and typically confined to the youngest or least-experienced workers. Larger disemployment effects show up mainly for much bigger increases or in a minority of studies that use different methods or samples.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Twin, adoption, and genomic studies converge on a substantial genetic contribution to individual differences in IQ within populations. Classical twin designs (including twins reared apart) and adoption designs typically estimate narrow-sense heritability in the range of roughly 50–80% by adulthood, with estimates rising from childhood into later life while shared-family environmental effects shrink toward zero. Genome-wide association studies and polygenic scores independently corroborate a genetic signal: common SNPs account for a sizable fraction of variance (SNP heritability often ~20–30%), and polygenic scores predict IQ differences even in within-family comparisons that reduce many environmental confounds. The three methods do not yield identical point estimates—genomic figures are lower because they capture only part of genetic variation—but they agree that genetic differences are a major source of IQ variation among people in a given population.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. The Great Depression began in 1929 (industrial production peaked mid-year; the stock-market crash came in October), while the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act was not signed until June 1930. It therefore cannot have caused the downturn’s onset.

It did contribute to the Depression’s depth and duration. The act raised U.S. import duties sharply, prompted retaliatory tariffs abroad, and helped shrink already-falling world trade. Most economic historians treat that trade contraction as a secondary aggravating factor, not the primary driver. Larger roles are assigned to the 1929 financial collapse, widespread bank failures, the Federal Reserve’s contractionary policy, and the constraints of the gold standard.

CONFIDENCE: 88

The interwar gold standard was a major amplifier of the Great Depression. Fixed gold parities and convertibility rules tied countries’ money supplies to gold reserves and forced them to defend those parities with high interest rates and monetary contraction whenever reserves were threatened. That transmitted deflation and banking stress across borders, limited lender-of-last-resort action, and turned an initial downturn into a deeper, more synchronized collapse.

Countries that left gold earlier regained monetary independence, often devalued, and recovered faster in output and prices. Britain (1931) and much of Scandinavia and the sterling bloc are the classic early cases; the United States’ 1933 suspension of gold convertibility likewise coincided with the start of recovery. Gold-bloc countries that stayed on gold into the mid-1930s (notably France) remained in deflation and stagnation longer. The timing of departure is one of the strongest cross-country predictors of the timing of recovery in the historical record.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Standard Oil’s refining market share was already eroding in the years before and around the 1911 dissolution (down from roughly 90% in the late nineteenth century toward the mid-60% range), while kerosene prices continued their long decline.

CONFIDENCE: 72

The “China shock” research (chiefly Autor, Dorn, and Hanson) found that the post-1990s surge in Chinese imports caused large, geographically concentrated, and persistent losses of U.S. manufacturing jobs. Local labor markets specialized in competing industries saw higher unemployment, lower labor-force participation, and reduced earnings that were not offset by gains in other local sectors; worker mobility and reallocation were slow and incomplete over a decade or more, and transfer payments rose. Later work in the same line linked these shocks to broader social and political effects.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Nearly half (per the causal estimates in Cutler & Miller 2005 for major U.S. cities, ~1900–1936). Clean-water filtration and chlorination account for that share of the overall urban mortality drop, a larger share of the infant and child mortality drops, and large reductions in typhoid in particular.

CONFIDENCE: 78

Yes. The Acid Rain Program under Title IV of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments cut power-plant SO2 far below the statutory cap, at much lower cost than projected, and produced large, measured drops in acid deposition.

The program capped utility SO2 and issued tradable allowances (Phase I from 1995 for the largest plants; Phase II from 2000 for virtually all fossil units), with a permanent cap near 8.95 million tons—roughly a 10-million-ton cut from 1980 levels. Covered sources emitted about 15.7 million tons in 1990; by the mid-2000s they were well under the cap, and by the mid-2010s emissions were on the order of 2–3 million tons. Allowance trading, banking, and fuel-switching/scrubber choices delivered those cuts. Ex-ante cost estimates often ran several billion dollars a year (sometimes cited near or above $6 billion); realized compliance costs were commonly estimated around $1–2 billion a year or less.

Ambient results tracked the emissions. Wet sulfate deposition across the eastern United States fell on the order of 50–70 percent from early-1990s levels. Many acidified lakes and streams, especially in the Northeast, became less acidic and showed biological improvement, though full recovery of soils and sensitive waters is slow and incomplete. Co-benefits from lower fine particulate matter (sulfate) were large relative to program costs. Later rules (CAIR, CSAPR, and tighter NAAQS) tightened interstate and health-based limits further; they built on, rather than repudiated, the cap-and-trade architecture.

Limitations do not overturn the result: NOx was handled separately and less completely at first; some ecosystems remain impaired; and allowance prices and politics shifted as the cap became non-binding under later regulations. On its own terms—SO2 emissions, deposition, and cost—the program is one of the clearest empirical successes of U.S. environmental policy.

CONFIDENCE: 90

Randomised evaluations (notably the cluster of RCTs summarised in the 2015 *American Economic Journal: Applied Economics* special issue, plus closely related trials) found that expanding access to microcredit produced only modest average effects. Borrowers were somewhat more likely to start or expand small businesses and to invest in them, but there were no statistically or economically large gains in household income, consumption, or other standard measures of poverty and living standards for the average recipient. Effects were heterogeneous—some existing entrepreneurs benefited more—but the programmes did not deliver the transformative poverty reduction often claimed for microcredit.

CONFIDENCE: 88

The 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments (and the pre-market safety rules that preceded them) require proof of safety and efficacy before a drug can be sold. That rule has blocked some dangerous or useless products and has given physicians and patients a stronger quality signal than pure post-market reputation and tort law would have supplied. Those gains are real but limited: many of the worst historical disasters were already constrainable under the 1938 safety statute, post-market surveillance and liability continue to catch problems the pre-market screen misses, and ineffective drugs are often revealed by clinical experience anyway.

The costs are larger and more systematic. Development times and out-of-pocket costs rose sharply after 1962; the flow of new chemical entities fell and never fully recovered; and the United States experienced a well-documented “drug lag” relative to peer countries. Econometric evaluations (starting with Peltzman 1973 and extended by later work on entry, lag, and consumer surplus) find that the lost health benefits from drugs that were delayed, never developed, or priced out of reach exceed the health benefits of the products kept off the market. The asymmetry is structural: approving a harmful drug produces visible victims and political punishment, while delaying or deterring a beneficial drug produces an invisible graveyard that does not show up in FDA statistics. Higher barriers also shift R&D toward incremental, lower-risk projects and raise prices for the drugs that do appear.

Later reforms (user fees, accelerated approval, priority review) have shortened some timelines but have not reversed the core tradeoff. On the available cost-benefit evidence, the net effect of mandatory pre-market approval has been to make Americans worse off.

CONFIDENCE: 62

Inflation stayed low and stable for roughly a decade after the Fed’s post-2008 large-scale asset purchases, generally running below the 2% target rather than accelerating into the runaway or hyperinflationary episode many critics forecast. The monetary base rose sharply, but that increase did not pass through into broad money or spending at anything like a one-for-one rate.

The quantity-theory prediction (a large rise in M produces a large rise in P) failed because two of its usual background assumptions broke down at once. Banks held the new reserves as excess balances at the Fed—encouraged by interest on excess reserves and by weak loan demand—so the money multiplier collapsed and broader aggregates such as M2 grew far more slowly than the base. At the same time, the velocity of money fell sharply as households, firms, and financial institutions increased their demand for safe, liquid assets amid deleveraging, elevated uncertainty, and a large output gap. With abundant slack and anchored inflation expectations, the extra base money mainly lowered long-term yields and supported asset prices rather than bidding up consumer prices. (The later 2021–22 inflation surge was driven by subsequent fiscal stimulus, supply shocks, and reopening dynamics, not by the 2008–14 QE programs themselves.)

CONFIDENCE: 88

The Federal Reserve was created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 mainly to address repeated banking panics (especially 1907) and the rigid currency and lack of a lender of last resort under the prior National Banking system. Its core aims were an elastic currency, centralized reserves, bank supervision, and emergency liquidity to limit runs and payment-system breakdowns; later statutes added an explicit dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices.

It has only partly met those aims. Classic deposit runs became rare after the 1930s once the Fed was paired with deposit insurance and stronger supervision, and post-1980s policy coincided with lower output volatility for a time (the so-called Great Moderation). Major failures remain clear: the Fed’s contractionary stance deepened the early-1930s collapse; 1970s policy allowed high inflation; and 2008 and 2021–22 showed that discretionary credit and balance-sheet policies can still permit severe financial stress and inflation overshoots. Banking and macroeconomic instability have not been eliminated, and whether net stability improved relative to a well-designed alternative regime remains contested.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Official estimates (notably the 2017 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report, along with CBO analyses) find that the net fiscal effect is modest relative to the U.S. economy and highly dependent on time horizon, government level, and immigrant education/skill. First-generation immigrants are typically a net fiscal cost—especially lower-skilled arrivals—because education and other services for them and their children exceed the taxes they pay, with the burden concentrated at the state and local level. Their U.S.-born children are strong net contributors. Over multi-decade horizons that include descendants, the overall effect is often near zero to modestly positive and is more favorable for higher-skilled immigrants; recent CBO work on immigration surges likewise projects net federal deficit reduction over a 10-year window because added revenues exceed added outlays.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Migrant remittances to low- and middle-income countries are substantially larger than official development assistance (ODA). In recent years they have run on the order of three times ODA (roughly $600+ billion versus roughly $200 billion annually), and they have exceeded aid since the late 1990s. They are now among the largest, and for many countries the largest, source of external finance.

Their economic profiles differ in several systematic ways. Remittances are private, person-to-person transfers that reach households directly; ODA is a public flow, usually government-to-government or via official institutions, and is often earmarked for projects, budget support, or policy conditions. Remittances are relatively stable and tend to be counter-cyclical (rising when home-country conditions worsen); aid is more volatile and shaped by donor politics and budgets. Remittances create no sovereign debt and are unconditional, whereas a large share of ODA has historically been loans or tied to donor priorities. Household use of remittances is concentrated on consumption smoothing, education, health, and small-scale investment; aid is more often directed at public goods, infrastructure, and institutional programs, with well-known problems of fungibility and governance. Transfer costs remain material for remittances, while aid effectiveness depends heavily on recipient institutions and donor design.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. The 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (which finished dismantling the Glass-Steagall separation of commercial and investment banking) was not a meaningful cause of the 2008 crisis.

The losses and failures that defined the crisis came from the housing bubble, subprime and Alt-A mortgage origination, securitization into MBS/CDOs, related credit derivatives, extreme leverage, and runs in the shadow-banking system. Those activities were not what Glass-Steagall prohibited, and they were carried out largely by firms the 1933 Act never constrained:

- Stand-alone investment banks (Bear Stearns, Lehman, Merrill Lynch, Goldman, Morgan Stanley) had always been outside Glass-Steagall; several failed or were rescued.
- AIG’s collapse was an insurance/derivatives problem.
- Major mortgage specialists (Countrywide and others) and the GSEs were not commercial-bank/investment-bank combinations created by the repeal.
- Even large universal banks that later needed support (e.g., Citigroup) lost money on mortgage-related securities and trading books they could largely have held under pre-1999 rules and loopholes; their commercial-banking franchises were not the source of the systemic break.

Glass-Steagall had already been heavily eroded by the 1980s–90s (Section 20 subsidiaries, etc.). Countries with long-standing universal banking also suffered large losses once U.S. mortgage securities and funding markets seized up. Post-crisis official and academic reviews (including the bulk of the economic literature and much of the FCIC record) locate the main drivers in housing credit, securitization and ratings, leverage and maturity transformation outside traditional banks, and supervisory failures around those markets—not in the 1999 affiliation rules.

The repeal was part of a broader deregulatory climate and may have modestly encouraged larger, more complex firms, but that is not the same as causing the crisis. Reinstating a strict separation would not have stopped the housing bubble or the shadow-bank run.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Yes. Federal deposit insurance (the FDIC system created in 1933–34) has, on net, stabilized U.S. banking by removing the main trigger for contagious depositor runs.

Before federal insurance, U.S. banking was punctuated by panics in which depositors ran even on solvent banks (notably 1873, 1893, 1907, and 1930–33). Those runs destroyed liquidity, forced fire sales, and amplified downturns; thousands of banks failed in the early 1930s alone. After insurance of small deposits, that mechanism largely disappeared. Insured depositors no longer had a first-mover incentive to withdraw, so isolated insolvencies stopped cascading into system-wide scrambles for cash. From the mid-1930s until the uninsured-deposit runs of 2023, the United States did not experience a classic nationwide banking panic of the pre-FDIC type, despite recessions, the S&L troubles, and 2008.

The offsetting cost is moral hazard: protected depositors monitor less, so banks can take more risk, and poorly priced insurance plus forbearance contributed to the scale of the 1980s thrift and bank failures. That cost is real and has required capital rules, supervision, and resolution authority to contain. It has not, however, restored the pre-1933 pattern of frequent runs on otherwise viable institutions. Episodes of stress have instead been managed by expanding coverage or guaranteeing uninsured liabilities precisely because the insured core remained stable.
